note: The -t is the accusative: the full form is 'Jó reggelt kívánok' (I wish [you] a good morning), so the greeting is the object of an unspoken verb. Stress, as always in Hungarian, falls on the first syllable.

example.en: Good morning! How did you sleep?

note: From 'este' (evening) plus accusative -t; the final e lengthens to é before the suffix. Used both when arriving and when meeting someone after about 6 pm.
'Éjszaka' (night) is itself a compound of 'éj' (night) and 'szak' (period). Said only when parting for the night, never as a greeting.
English loan, written with a long ó as Hungarian spelling requires. Informal, like 'szia'; among young people it also serves as 'bye'.
'Szia' takes the 2nd person plural ending -sztok, as if it were a verb, so you greet a group differently from one person. Informal only.
'Vagy' is the 2nd person singular of 'van' (to be). The usual answers are 'Jól' (well), 'Köszönöm, jól' or 'Megvagyok' (I'm getting by).

example.en: Hi! How are you? – Fine, thanks.

note: Formal address in Hungarian uses 3rd person verb forms with 'ön' or 'maga' (you), so the polite 'how are you' is literally 'how is he/she'.
'Szépen' is the adverb of 'szép' (beautiful, nice). 'Köszönöm' is the definite form 'I thank it'; a more neutral 'thanks' is 'köszönöm' alone.
Clipped from 'köszönöm' with the affectionate -i ending that Hungarian also uses for nicknames. Casual; 'kösz' is even shorter.
From 'szív' (heart) + -es (adjective) + -en (adverb): literally 'with heart'. Also means 'gladly' in 'Szívesen segítek' (I'll gladly help).
A noun from the verb 'bocsát' (to let go, to forgive). Use it to apologise or to get past someone; 'Bocsánat, hogy...' = 'sorry that...'.
From 'elnéz' (to overlook, to let pass) + -és (noun) + -t (accusative): 'I ask for [your] overlooking'. The standard way to stop a stranger or a waiter.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

note: Hungarians often answer by repeating the verb instead: 'Jössz? – Jövök.' (Are you coming? – I'm coming.) 'Igen' alone can sound a little curt.
Both the answer 'no' and the negator 'not', placed right before the word it negates: 'nem tudom' (I don't know). 'Nem' also means 'gender, sex' and 'kind' as a noun.
'Legyen' is the formal imperative of 'van' (be) and 'szíves' is 'hearted, kind' from 'szív' (heart). Informal equivalent: 'légy szíves'. Often follows the request.
1st person of the slightly old-fashioned verb 'örvend' (to rejoice). Hungarians give the family name first when introducing themselves.

example.en: Pleased to meet you, I'm Anna Kovács.

note: 'Étvágy' is a compound of 'ét' (food, as in 'étel') and 'vágy' (desire). Said before eating, including by waiters; the reply is 'köszönöm' or the same back.
'Út' means road, way or journey; its ú shortens to u before the accusative -t (út → utat), a common vowel-shortening pattern.
Same pattern as 'Jó napot', with 'szép' (beautiful). Common from shop assistants and waiters as you leave; 'További szép napot' = 'enjoy the rest of your day'.
From 'üdv' (salvation, hail) with the verb ending -öl and the definite 1st person -öm. Formal spoken greeting and the opening of letters: 'Tisztelt Uram!' is the written equivalent.
'Semmi' is 'nothing' and 'baj' is 'trouble'. Reply to an apology; 'Nem baj' (not trouble) means 'it doesn't matter'.
The 3rd person imperative of 'tetszik' (to please). Used when handing something over, inviting someone in, answering the phone, and as 'Tessék?' for 'Pardon?'.

example.en: Here you are, here's the key.

note: 'Hívnak' is 3rd person plural ('they call'), the Hungarian way of making an impersonal sentence. Formal: 'Hogy hívják?'. Answer: '... vagyok' (I am ...).

en: Hello / goodbye to an elder (said by children)
note: Short for 'kezét csókolom' (I kiss your hand), the old courtly greeting. Today children say it to adults, and adults to much older women; otherwise it sounds dated.
Clipped from 'viszontlátásra' (until seeing again): 'viszont' (again, in return) + 'lát' (see). Less formal than the full form but still fine with strangers.
From Latin 'nulla' (none). On the phone and in scores you may also hear 'zéró'.
Also the indefinite article 'a / an': 'egy könyv' = a book. Pronounced with a long 'gy' sound ('eggy') when stressed as a number.
'Kettő' stands alone; before a noun it is 'két' ('két jegy' = two tickets). People say 'kettő' when dictating numbers so it is not mistaken for 'hét' (seven). Cognate with Finnish 'kaksi'.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'kolme'. The 'három' stem shortens to 'harm-' in 'harminc' (30) and 'harmadik' (third).
Cognate with Finnish 'neljä'. Hungarian nouns stay singular after numbers: 'négy alma' (four apple), never 'almák'.
Cognate with Finnish 'viisi'. 'Ötven' (50) is built from it with the suffix -ven.
Cognate with Finnish 'kuusi'. 'Hat' is also the verb 'to have an effect' (hat valamire), but context keeps them apart.
'Hét' also means 'week' (a 'seven-day'). In 'hetven' (70) and the plural 'hetek' the long é shortens to e.
The 'ny' is a single sound, like the 'ny' in 'canyon'; 'c' is pronounced 'ts'. 'Nyolcvan' = 80.
Final 'c' sounds like 'ts'. 'Kilencven' = 90.
An ancient Iranian loanword (compare Ossetic 'dæs', Persian 'dah'), like 'száz' and 'ezer'. The í shortens in 'tizen-' (ten-plus) and 'tized' (tenth).
'Tizen' is 'tíz' plus the locative -en: 'one on ten'. All of 11–19 follow this pattern: tizenkettő, tizenhárom, ... tizenkilenc.
Before a noun it becomes 'tizenkét': 'tizenkét óra' (twelve o'clock).
21–29 use the shortened form 'huszon-': huszonegy, huszonkettő. The long ú becomes short u there.
Built on the short stem 'harm-' of 'három'. From 40 upward the tens take -van/-ven instead: negyven, ötven, hatvan, hetven, nyolcvan, kilencven.
'Négy' + -ven, with the é shortened to e. The suffix obeys vowel harmony: -van after back vowels (hatvan), -ven after front vowels (negyven).
'Öt' + -ven. Prices are often given in hundreds: 'ötven' alone rarely means forints, 'ötszáz' (500) does.
Iranian loanword (compare Persian 'sad', Sanskrit 'śata'). 'Kétszáz' = 200, 'százötven' = 150; no 'and' is inserted.
Iranian loanword (compare Persian 'hezār'). 'Kétezer' = 2000; in writing, numbers above 2000 are hyphenated at thousands: 'kétezer-huszonhat'.
Irregular: not from 'egy' but from 'el' (front, forward), so literally 'the front one'. Written '1.' with a full stop: '1. emelet' = first floor.
Irregular: built on 'más' (other), not on 'kettő'. 'Másik' means 'the other one'.
From 'három' onward ordinals are regular: stem + -adik/-edik/-odik/-ödik (negyedik, ötödik, hatodik, tizedik). Dates use them: 'május harmadika' = 3 May.
Clock times count toward the next hour: 'fél nyolc' (half eight) means 7:30. 'Fél' is also the verb 'to fear' and the root of 'feleség' (wife, 'one's other half').

example.en: Half a kilo of bread, please.

note: From German 'Paar'. 'Egy pár cipő' = a pair of shoes; 'pár perc' = a few minutes. Also 'partner' in 'párom' (my partner).

example.en: I'll come in a few minutes.

note: Used for countable things; 'mennyi' is 'how much'. The noun stays singular: 'Hány gyerek?' (how many child). 'Hány éves vagy?' asks someone's age.
A Slavic loanword (compare Old Slavic 'čeljadь', household). 'Családi' = family (adj.): 'családi ház' = detached house.
Possessive forms are the usual way to say it: 'anyám' (my mother), 'anyja' (his/her mother). 'Anyu' and 'anyuka' are the affectionate 'mum'.
'Apám' = my father, 'apja' = his/her father. The final short a lengthens to á before most suffixes (apa → apák, apát).
Pet form of 'anya' with the nursery ending -u; 'anyuka' and 'anyuci' are even more affectionate. Used as a form of address: 'Anyu!'.
Pet form of 'apa', parallel to 'anyu'. 'Apuka' and 'apuci' are also common.
The present participle of 'szül' (to give birth), so it names the parent by the act of bearing a child. 'Szüleim' = my parents.
'Gyermek' is the formal or literary form of the same word. Plural 'gyerekek'; 'gyerekkor' = childhood. The 'gy' is one sound, roughly 'dy'.
Means both 'boy' and 'son'; 'fiam' = my son. Finno-Ugric word related to Finnish 'poika' (boy). The ú shortens in 'fiuk' (their son), but 'fiúk' is the plural 'boys'.
Both 'girl' and 'daughter'; 'lányom' = my daughter. The 'ny' is a single palatal sound. 'Leány' is the older, literary form.
A compound of 'test' (body) and 'vér' (blood): someone of the same flesh and blood. Hungarian has no plain word for brother or sister without saying older or younger.
Almost always used with a possessive: 'bátyám' (my older brother), 'bátyja'. Hungarian always marks whether a sibling is older or younger.
'Öcsém' = my younger brother; also a slangy way to address a mate ('öcsém!', like 'bro'). Pair: 'báty' (older brother).
'Nő' (woman) + 'vér' (blood). The same word means 'nurse' in hospitals ('nővér', 'ápolónő'). Younger sister is a different word, 'húg'.
'Húgom' = my younger sister. The four sibling words (báty, öcs, nővér, húg) encode both sex and relative age; 'testvér' is the neutral cover term.
'Nagy' (big, great) + 'mama'. 'Nagyi' is the cosy 'granny'; 'nagyanya' is the more formal term.
'Nagy' + 'papa'; the formal term is 'nagyapa'. 'Nagyszülők' = grandparents.
A Slavic loan (compare Slovak 'vnuk'). Also the base of cousin words: 'unokatestvér' (cousin, literally 'grandchild-sibling').
From 'fél' (half, partner) + -ség: one's other half. 'Feleségem' = my wife. The everyday 'nejem' (my wife) is a shorter alternative.
'Férjem' = my husband. Related to 'férfi' (man). 'Férjhez megy' (goes to a husband) is what a woman does when she marries; a man 'megnősül'.
Means 'human being' and, in the plural 'emberek', 'people'. 'Az emberek' = people in general; 'emberi' = human (adj.).
Also a verb: 'nő' means 'grows'. As a suffix -nő marks female versions of jobs: 'tanárnő' (female teacher). Finno-Ugric, related to Finnish 'nainen'.
An old compound of 'férj' (man, husband) and 'fi' (son). 'Férfiak' = men. In toilets you'll see 'Férfi' and 'Női' (women's).
Also means 'doll'. 'Kisbaba' (little baby) makes it unambiguous. 'Babázik' = plays with dolls.
'Néni' alone is how children address any older woman ('Kati néni'). 'Nagynéni' is specifically a parent's sister.
'Bácsi' is any older man to a child ('Pista bácsi'); 'nagybácsi' is the family uncle. The 'cs' is pronounced 'ch'.
The é shortens before suffixes: 'kenyeret' (acc.), 'kenyerek'. 'Egy szelet kenyér' = a slice of bread. Hungarian white loaves are often sold by the half kilo.
'Tejföl' (milk-top) is the sour cream used in many Hungarian dishes; 'tejeskávé' = coffee with milk.
Remember 's' is pronounced 'sh' in Hungarian, so 'sajt' sounds like 'shoyt'. 'Sajtos' = with cheese.
From the verb 'tojik' (to lay eggs) + -ás. 'Rántotta' = scrambled eggs, 'tükörtojás' (mirror-egg) = fried egg.
'Húsleves' = meat soup (the Sunday clear broth). The ú shortens in some forms: 'húst' keeps it, but 'husi' is baby talk for meat.
'Csirkepaprikás' (chicken paprikash) is one of the best-known dishes. 'Cs' = 'ch'. 'Tyúk' is the hen as an animal.
A textbook Finno-Ugric cognate: Finnish 'kala', Estonian 'kala'. 'Halászlé' (fisherman's soup) is the spicy paprika fish soup.
A Turkic loan from the pre-conquest period (compare Turkish 'yemiş'). 'Gyümölcslé' = fruit juice, literally 'fruit-juice'.
From 'zöld' (green) + -ség. Also used as an insult meaning 'nonsense' ('zöldségeket beszél' = talks rubbish).
A Turkic loanword (Turkish 'elma', Kazakh 'alma'), one of many farming words borrowed before the Hungarians settled the Carpathian Basin. 'Almalé' = apple juice.
Colloquial, from Austrian German 'Grundbirne' (ground-pear) via dialect 'Krumbir'. The formal word on menus is 'burgonya'.
'Zs' is one letter, pronounced like the 's' in 'measure'. 'Rizses' = with rice.
From 'lé' (juice, liquid) + -es: 'the juicy thing'. Soup is a standard first course of a Hungarian lunch; 'gulyásleves' is the real goulash.
From Ottoman Turkish 'kahve', a legacy of the 150-year Turkish occupation. 'Kávézó' = café; 'egy kávét' is the accusative you order with.
Pronounced 'TE-a', two syllables. Takes back-vowel suffixes despite the spelling: 'teát' (acc.), 'teában'.
Pronounced 'shör'. 'Egy korsó sör' is a pint-sized mug, 'egy pohár sör' a smaller glass. 'Csapolt sör' = draught beer.
An Old Turkic loanword ('bor', wine). 'Vörösbor' = red wine, 'fehérbor' = white wine; 'fröccs' is the wine spritzer.
From German 'Zucker'. The o drops before suffixes: 'cukrot' (acc.), 'cukros' (sugary). 'Cukrászda' = pastry shop.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'suola'. The ó shortens in 'sót' (acc.) and 'sós' (salty).
From Serbo-Croatian, a diminutive of 'papar' (pepper). Means both the fresh pepper and the ground red spice; English borrowed the word from Hungarian.
From 'gulya' (herd of cattle) + -ás: the cattle herder. The dish is properly 'gulyásleves' (herdsman's soup) and is a soup, not the stew foreigners expect; that is 'pörkölt'.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'voi'. 'Vajas kenyér' = bread and butter.
A Slavic loan (compare Polish 'kiełbasa'). 'Virsli' is the thin frankfurter type; 'szalámi' is salami.
From the stem 'é-' of 'eszik' (to eat) + -tel. 'Ételek' = dishes on a menu; 'ennivaló' (thing-for-eating) is 'something to eat'.
From the stem 'i-' of 'iszik' (to drink) + -tal, parallel to 'étel'. 'Italok' heads the drinks section of a menu; 'üdítő' = soft drink.
'Ét' (food) + 'terem' (hall). The e of 'terem' drops before suffixes: 'étteremben' (in the restaurant) but 'éttermek' (restaurants).

example.en: Is there a good restaurant here?

note: From 'kávé' with the verb-forming -z and participle -ó: 'the coffee-doing one'. 'Kávéház' is the grand old coffee house.
'Ét' (food) + 'lap' (sheet, page). 'Itallap' is the drinks list. Note: 'menü' means the set meal of the day, not the card.
Coined in the 19th-century language reform from 'pince' (cellar, a Slavic loan): the one who fetches from the cellar. 'Pincérnő' = waitress.
From 'szám' (number). Also 'invoice' and 'bank account'. In a restaurant ask 'A számlát kérem' or 'Fizetek!' (I'm paying).
A Slavic loanword (compare Russian 'stol', Slovak 'stôl'), with an added initial a- because Old Hungarian avoided st- clusters. 'Asztalt foglalni' = to book a table.

example.en: I'd like to book a table for two.

note: From 'rend' (order, arrangement). With a specific object it takes the definite conjugation: 'rendelem a levest' (I order the soup). 'Megrendel' = to place an order.
'Fizetek!' is the normal way to call for the bill. Definite forms: fizetem, fizeted, fizeti ('kifizetem a számlát' = I'll pay the bill). 'Fizetés' = payment and also salary.
The all-purpose ordering verb: 'Egy sört kérek' = a beer, please. Its definite form 'kérem' is the polite 'please' / 'you're welcome'. 'Kérsz valamit?' = do you want something?
An -ik verb with an irregular stem: 'iszom' (I drink), past 'ittam'. Its i- root is Finno-Ugric (Finnish 'juoda'). Definite: 'iszom a sört'. 'Ital' (drink) comes from it.
Irregular -ik verb; the 1st person ends in -m ('eszem', not 'eszek', in careful speech). Past 'ettem', infinitive 'enni'. Finno-Ugric root (Finnish 'syödä'). Definite: 'eszem a levest'.
'Reggel' (morning) + the adjective suffix -i, used as a noun. 'Reggelizik' = to have breakfast. Hotels advertise 'reggelivel' = with breakfast.
A Slavic loan (compare Russian 'obed'). Traditionally the main hot meal of the day, often soup plus a main. 'Ebédel' = to have lunch; 'ebédszünet' = lunch break.
A Slavic loan (compare Czech 'večeře'). 'Vacsorázik' = to have dinner; 'vacsorára' = for dinner.
The á shortens before suffixes: 'poharat' (acc.), 'poharak'. 'Egy pohár víz' = a glass of water; 'pohárköszöntő' = a toast.
'Egy csésze kávé' = a cup of coffee. Note the two 'cs' sounds; the final e lengthens before suffixes: 'csészét'.
'Lapostányér' = flat plate, 'mélytányér' (deep plate) = soup plate. Plural 'tányérok'.
Same spelling as 'villa' (the house) and the root of 'villám' (lightning) and 'villamos' (tram, originally 'electric'). Context decides.
Pronounced 'kaysh'. Do not confuse with 'kész' (ready) or 'kéz' (hand); only the final consonant differs.
The á shortens before suffixes: 'kanalat', 'kanalak'. 'Kiskanál' = teaspoon, 'evőkanál' (eating-spoon) = tablespoon.
'Bor' (wine) + -ra (for) + 'való' (meant): money meant for wine. Around 10% is usual; say the total you want to pay when handing over cash, as change is not always brought back.
From French 'dessert' via German; the doubled 'ssz' writes a long 's' sound. Classic choices: 'somlói galuska', 'palacsinta' (crêpes), 'rétes' (strudel).
Because the object is definite ('a számlát'), the verb takes the definite ending -em ('kérem'), not 'kérek'. A good illustration of Hungary's two conjugations.
Indefinite object ('egy kávét'), so the verb is the indefinite 'kérek'. Swap in any item: 'egy sört kérek', 'egy teát kérek'.
From Latin 'finus' via German 'fein'; means both 'delicious' and 'fine, delicate'. 'Nagyon finom!' is the compliment every host hopes to hear.
Highly irregular: 'megyek, mész, megy, megyünk, mentek, mennek'; infinitive 'menni', past 'mentem'. The 2nd person 'mész' has no -sz ending visible because the stem itself ends in sz.
Irregular: the stem becomes 'jöv-' in 'jövök, jövünk' and the infinitive 'jönni'; past 'jöttem'. 'Jövő' (coming) also means 'the future'.
From 'út' (road) + the verb-former -az + -ik. An -ik verb, so 'I travel' is 'utazom'. 'Utazás' = journey, 'utas' = passenger.

example.en: We're travelling to Vienna by train.

note: Because the stem ends in -s, the 2nd person singular is 'keresel', not 'keressz'. Also 'to earn' (money): 'jól keres' = earns well. Definite: 'keresem a kulcsot'.

example.en: I'm looking for the railway station.

note: From 'ér' (to reach) + -kez + -ik. Use it with -ba/-be or -ra/-re for the destination: 'Budapestre érkezik'. 'Érkezés' on airport boards = arrivals.
The ú shortens before many suffixes: 'utat', 'utak', 'utam'. Appears in 'útlevél' (passport), 'utazik' (travel) and the street type 'út' (avenue): 'Andrássy út'.
A Slavic loan (compare Polish 'ulica'); the older spelling 'utcza' survives on some signs. Written after the name: 'Váci utca'. 'Az utcán' = in the street.
Basic meaning 'space'; a town square is a 'space' in the city. Follows the name on signs: 'Deák Ferenc tér'. Location: 'a téren' (on the square).
'Tér' (space) + 'kép' (picture), a transparent compound coined in the language reform. 'Útitérkép' = road map.
'Jobb' means both 'right (side)' and 'better' (comparative of 'jó'), as in many languages. The suffix -ra gives direction; 'jobb oldalon' = on the right side.

example.en: Turn right at the second street.

note: 'Bal' + -ra. 'Bal' carries the usual 'sinister' overtones: 'balszerencse' = bad luck, 'baleset' = accident ('left-fall').
'Egyenes' (straight, built on 'egy', one, as in 'of one line') + the adverb ending -en. 'Menjen egyenesen tovább' = carry straight on.
Front-vowel 'itt' = here, back-vowel 'ott' = there; Hungarian often pairs near/far words this way (ez/az, ide/oda, így/úgy). 'Ide' = to here (motion).
Counterpart of 'itt'. 'Oda' = to there, 'onnan' = from there. 'Ott van' = it's over there.
From 'köz' (gap, between). Takes the -hoz/-hez/-höz case: 'közel a parkhoz' (near the park). 'Közelebb' = closer.
'Messze van?' = is it far? Takes -tól/-től: 'messze a várostól' (far from the city). 'Messzi' is the adjective form.
'Hol' asks about location only; 'hova / hová' (to where) and 'honnan' (from where) exist separately, because Hungarian keeps place, motion-to and motion-from apart.
A language-reform coinage from 'száll' (to alight, to lodge) + -oda, the same suffix as in 'iroda' (office). 'Hotel' is also used; 'szállás' = accommodation.
'Út' (road) + 'levél' (letter, also 'leaf'): the document that lets you travel. Plural 'útlevelek' with the é shortened.
Basic meaning 'mark, sign', hence also 'school grade' and 'engagement' ('eljegyzés'). 'Jegypénztár' = ticket office, 'jegyet venni' = to buy a ticket.

example.en: Where can I buy a ticket?

note: From 'bőr' (leather, skin) + the reform-era suffix -önd. 'Csomag' = luggage or parcel; 'kézipoggyász' = hand luggage.
From 'nyár' (summer): 'nyaral' is 'to spend the summer away', so a holiday is literally a 'summering'. 'Szabadság' (freedom) is leave from work.
Means both a national border and a 'limit' ('határidő' = deadline, literally 'limit-time'). 'Határátkelő' = border crossing.
The prefix 'el-' (away) + 'téved' (to err, to go wrong) + past tense -tem. 'Tévedés' = mistake; 'eltévedtünk' = we're lost.
The o drops before suffixes: 'a sarkon' = at the corner, 'sarkok'. The same word means 'heel' (of foot or shoe).

example.en: There is a bank on the corner.

note: Clipped from 'autóbusz'. Means of transport take the suffix -val/-vel ('with'): 'busszal' = by bus, with the v assimilated to the final consonant.

example.en: I go to work by bus.

note: Short for 'villamos vasút' (electric railway); 'villamos' is the adjective from 'villany' (electricity). Budapest's yellow trams on lines 4 and 6 are among the busiest in Europe.
Budapest's M1 (1896) is the oldest underground line on the European mainland. 'Metróval' = by metro; 'metróállomás' = metro station.
A 19th-century coinage from 'von' (to pull, to draw) + -at: the thing that is drawn along. 'Vonattal' = by train; 'gyorsvonat' = fast train.
'Pálya' (track, course, career) + 'udvar' (yard, a Slavic loan). Budapest has Keleti (Eastern), Nyugati (Western) and Déli (Southern) pályaudvar. Short: 'pu.'.
From 'megáll' (to stop, 'meg-' + 'áll' stand) + the participle -ó. 'A következő megálló' = the next stop, the phrase you hear on every tram.

example.en: At which stop should I get off?

note: From German 'Auto'. 'Autóval' = by car; 'autópálya' (car-track) = motorway. The older formal word 'gépkocsi' (machine-coach) survives in official texts.
Pronounced 'TOK-si'. Suffixes follow the written i: 'taxival' (by taxi), 'taxit hívni' = to call a taxi.
Colloquial, from 'bicycle' via Austrian German; the official word is 'kerékpár' (wheel-pair). 'Biciklizik' = to cycle; 'bringa' is slang.
'Repülő' (flying, from 'repül') + 'gép' (machine). In speech it is shortened to 'repülő' or just 'gép': 'a gép késik' = the plane is late.
'Repülő' + 'tér' (space, square). Budapest's airport is 'Liszt Ferenc repülőtér'; the colloquial 'reptér' is a clipped form.
'Hajóval' = by boat. 'Hajózik' = to sail. In Budapest 'hajó' also names the public river boats on the Danube that take normal tickets.
From 'bér' (rent, wage) + -let: something rented for a period. 'Havi bérlet' = monthly pass, 'diákbérlet' = student pass. Also a season ticket for the theatre.
'Menet' (going, run, from 'megy') + 'rend' (order). 'Menetjegy' is the formal word for a travel ticket.
Primary meaning 'to lead' (a 'vezető' is a leader or a driver). 'Autót vezet' = drives a car. 'Jogosítvány' = driving licence.
'Fel' (up) + 'száll' (to fly, to alight). The prefix separates in some sentences: 'nem száll fel' (doesn't get on). Takes -ra/-re: 'felszáll a buszra'.
'Le' (down) + 'száll'. Takes -ról/-ről: 'leszáll a villamosról'. 'Leszállás' = alighting, and also an aircraft's landing.

example.en: I'm getting off at the next one.

note: Also the noun 'castle, fortress' (Budai Vár). Transitive: 'várom a buszt' (definite). Takes -ra/-re with a person or event: 'várok rád' = I'm waiting for you.
'Indulás' on station boards = departures. Also 'to start' in general: 'indul a tanév' (the school year starts). 'Elindul' = to set off.

example.en: When does the next bus leave?

note: Strictly the track, but announcements use it for the platform: 'a vonat a harmadik vágányról indul' = the train leaves from track 3. 'Peron' is the platform surface.
From 'késő' (late). An -ik verb: 'késem' = I'm late. Also of clocks: 'késik az órám' = my watch is slow. 'Késés' = delay.

example.en: The train is ten minutes late.

note: From German 'Benzin'. 'Benzinkút' (petrol-well) = petrol station; 'tankol' = to fill up. Diesel is 'gázolaj' or just 'dízel'.
From 'parkol' (to park) + -ó, the same participle used in 'megálló' and 'kávézó'. 'Parkolni tilos' = no parking.
From French 'chauffeur' via German, respelled phonetically. 'Buszsofőr' = bus driver; the native 'vezető' also works, and 'járművezető' is the official term.
'Át' (across, over) + 'száll'. 'Átszállás' = a change / connection; 'át kell szállni' = you have to change. The prefix detaches: 'Hol szállok át?' = Where do I change?

example.target: A Deák téren szállj át a kettesre.
example.en: Change to line 2 at Deák tér.

note: One word for both 'time' and 'weather': 'Nincs időm' = I have no time; 'Milyen az idő?' = What's the weather like? Before suffixes the ő shortens: 'idők', 'időt'.
Ultimately from Latin 'hora'. Means hour, clock or watch, and a lesson at school. 'Három óra' = 3 o'clock or three hours; 'három órakor' = at 3.
'Egy perc' = one minute, 'öt perc múlva' = in five minutes. 'Perc' and 'másodperc' (second, literally 'second-minute') are both 19th-century coinages.
One word for both 'day' and 'sun': 'napkelte' = sunrise, 'három nap' = three days. 'Napos' = sunny, 'napi' = daily, 'naponta' = every day.
'Hét' (week) + 'vége' (its end, with the possessive -e). 'Hétvégén' = at the weekend; 'szép hétvégét!' = have a nice weekend.

example.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

note: 'Hó' (moon, month) + 'nap' (day). 'Hó' alone also means 'snow', so 'hónap' avoids the confusion; months are named with 'hó' in dates: 'május hó'.
'Éves' = years old ('tíz éves' = ten years old); 'évente' = yearly; 'tanév' = school year. 'Esztendő' is a literary synonym.
'Mai' = today's ('a mai nap' = this day). 'Ma este' = tonight, 'ma reggel' = this morning.
An old word 'hol' (dawn, morning) + 'nap' (day). 'Holnapután' = the day after tomorrow, 'holnap reggel' = tomorrow morning.
An old element 'teg' + 'nap'. 'Tegnapelőtt' = the day before yesterday, 'tegnap este' = last night.
'Most' = now; 'mostanában' = these days, 'pont most' = right now. Not to be confused with English 'most'.
Both the noun and the adverb 'in the morning': 'reggel hétkor' = at 7 in the morning. 'Reggeli' = breakfast.
Means 'noon' and 'south', because the sun stands in the south at midday. 'Délben' = at noon, 'délelőtt' = morning (before-noon), 'Dél-Amerika' = South America.
'Dél' (noon) + 'után' (after), the mirror of English 'afternoon'. 'Délután háromkor' = at 3 pm; 'du.' in written times.
'Ma este' = tonight, 'tegnap este' = last night. Takes the accusative in the greeting 'jó estét'. 'Esti' = evening (adj.).
'Hét' (week) + 'fő' (head): the head of the week. Days take -n for 'on': 'hétfőn' = on Monday. Day names are not capitalised in Hungarian.
From 'ketted', an old ordinal of 'kettő' (two): the second day. 'Kedden' = on Tuesday.
A Slavic loan meaning 'middle' (compare Russian 'sreda'): the middle of the week. 'Szerdán' = on Wednesday.
Slavic loan from 'fourth' (compare Slovak 'štvrtok'). 'Csütörtökön' = on Thursday.
Slavic loan from 'fifth' (compare Slovene 'petek'). Wednesday to Friday are all Slavic counting names. 'Pénteken' = on Friday.
From Slavic 'sobota', ultimately Hebrew 'shabbat'. 'Szombaton' = on Saturday.
'Vásár' (market, fair, a Persian loan related to 'bazaar') + 'nap' (day): the day of the weekly market. 'Vasárnap' alone also means 'on Sunday'.
Answer with the number plus 'óra': 'Hat óra van' (it's six). Half hours look ahead: 'fél hét' = 6:30, 'negyed hét' = 6:15, 'háromnegyed hét' = 6:45.
Month names are Latin-based and not capitalised: január, február, március, április, május, június, július, augusztus, szeptember, október, november, december. 'Januárban' = in January.
Comparative of 'késő' (late) with the -bb ending that all comparatives take. 'Majd később' = later on; 'legkésőbb' = at the latest.
Also 'surface' and 'stage' ('színház' = theatre, literally 'stage-house'). 'Milyen színű?' = what colour is it? 'Színes' = colourful.
Hungarian has two reds. 'Piros' is the everyday bright red (traffic lights, apples, tomatoes); 'vörös' is darker and reserved for blood, wine, hair, foxes and politics.
Related to 'vér' (blood). 'Vörösbor' = red wine, 'vöröshagyma' = onion, 'vörös haj' = red hair, 'Vöröskereszt' = Red Cross. For a red car or dress use 'piros'.
'Világoskék' = light blue, 'sötétkék' = dark blue. The Danube is 'a kék Duna' only in Strauss; locals know it is brown.
'Zöldség' (green-stuff) = vegetables; 'a zöldek' = the Greens (party). 'Zöld utat kap' = gets the green light.
An Old Turkic loanword (compare Turkish 'sarı'). The yellow trams of Budapest are 'a sárga villamos'. 'Sárgarépa' (yellow-turnip) = carrot.
'Fehérbor' = white wine, 'fehérnemű' (white-stuff) = underwear. Also a common surname.
'Fekete kávé' is black coffee, often just 'egy feketét' (a black one). Also a frequent surname (Fekete).
'Barna kenyér' = brown bread, 'barna haj' = brown hair. 'Barnul' = to get a tan (to 'brown').
Also 'dull, ordinary': 'szürke hétköznapok' = dreary weekdays. The 'ü' is like the French 'u' or German 'ü'.
'Narancs' (the fruit, via Italian 'arancia' from Persian) + 'sárga' (yellow). In casual speech 'narancs' alone can name the colour.
'Rózsa' (rose, a Slavic/Latin loan) + 'szín' (colour). Colour compounds with 'szín' are common: 'bordó' (claret) is a loan from French.
From German 'lila', ultimately Persian 'līlak' (lilac). 'Lila gőze sincs' (hasn't even purple steam) = hasn't the faintest idea.
From 'világ', which means both 'light' and 'world' (as in 'világ' = the lit world). 'Világoskék' = light blue; 'Világos?' = Is that clear?
'Sötétzöld' = dark green. 'Sötét van' = it's dark. Also 'dim-witted' when applied to a person.
Also 'round' (of drinks or a race) and 'club, circle' of people ('olvasókör' = reading circle). 'Körül' = around, 'környék' = surroundings.
A reform-era coinage from 'négy' (four) + -zet; also 'square' in maths ('négyzetméter' = square metre). A town square is 'tér'.
'Három' (three) + 'szög' (angle, nail). 'Négyszög' = quadrilateral, 'sokszög' (many-angle) = polygon.
From 'von' (to draw, to pull) + -al, like 'vonat' (train). Also a phone or transport line: 'a kettes vonal' = line 2.
From Latin 'punctum' via German 'Punkt'. Also the full stop, a score point, and an adverb 'exactly': 'pont most' = right now, 'pont ezt' = exactly this.
'Alakú' = -shaped ('kör alakú' = circular). Colloquially a 'guy': 'furcsa alak' = odd character. 'Alakít' = to shape, to act a role.
'Csillagos' = starry; 'csillagjegy' = star sign. Hotel ratings: 'négycsillagos szálloda' = four-star hotel.
An ancient Iranian loanword (compare Avestan 'zaranya'). Both the metal and the colour: 'aranysárga' = golden yellow. 'Aranyos' = cute, sweet.
Both the metal and the colour: 'ezüstszürke' = silver grey. 'Ezüstérem' = silver medal.
Of a mixed or patterned colour: 'tarka tehén' = a spotted cow, 'tarkabarka' = gaudy, motley.
'Testvér' (body-blood) = sibling; 'testnevelés' (body-education) = PE at school. Front-vowel word: 'testem' = my body.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'pää'. 'Fáj a fejem' = my head aches. Also a counting word: 'két fő' (two persons) uses the related 'fő'.
Only hair on the head; body hair is 'szőr'. 'Hajvágás' = haircut, 'fodrász' = hairdresser. Usually singular: 'szőke haja van' = has blond hair.
Cognate with Finnish 'silmä'. Paired body parts are singular in Hungarian: 'kék a szeme' = his/her eyes are blue; one eye is 'fél szem' (half an eye). Also 'grain, piece': 'egy szem szőlő'.
Like 'szem', used in the singular for the pair: 'fáj a fülem' = my ear(s) hurt. Also a 'handle' of a cup or bag.
The double 'rr' is pronounced long. 'Orrom' = my nose; 'orvos' (doctor) is unrelated despite the look.
Cognate with Finnish 'suu'. 'Szájam' = my mouth; 'szájharmonika' (mouth-harmonica) = harmonica. Do not confuse with 'száj'-like 'szál' (thread) or 'szó' (word).
Also the verb 'to hold, to catch' and the future auxiliary ('fogok menni' = I will go). 'Fogorvos' = dentist, 'fogkefe' = toothbrush.
'Nyakkendő' (neck-cloth) = tie, 'nyaklánc' (neck-chain) = necklace. 'Nyakon' = on the neck.
Cognate with Finnish 'käsi'. The é shortens before suffixes: 'kezem' (my hand), 'kezek'. Often covers the whole arm; 'kézzel' = by hand.
Also 'faculty' of a university and 'choir'. 'Karóra' (arm-clock) = wristwatch. 'Karom' = my arm, but 'karom' is also 'claw'.
One word for leg and foot; 'lábfej' (leg-head) is specifically the foot. 'Gyalog' = on foot, 'lábujj' = toe (leg-finger).
Cognate with Finnish 'sydän'. The root of 'szívesen' (gladly) and 'szíves' (kind). Also the verb 'to suck, to inhale': 'cigarettát szív' = smokes.
'Fáj a hátam' = my back hurts. The same word is the filler particle 'well, so': 'Hát, nem tudom' = Well, I don't know.
Pronounced 'hosh'. 'Hasfájás' = stomach ache (the everyday word); 'gyomor' is the medical stomach. 'Hasam' = my belly.
'Orvoshoz megyek' = I'm going to the doctor. 'Háziorvos' = GP, 'fogorvos' = dentist. 'Doktor' is used as a title: 'doktor úr'.
'Kór' (disease) + 'ház' (house). 'Kórházban van' = is in hospital. 'Kórterem' = hospital ward.
'Gyógy' (healing, as in 'gyógyfürdő', thermal bath) + 'szer' (agent, means). 'Gyógyít' = to cure, 'gyógyul' = to recover.
'Gyógyszer' + 'tár' (store, repository). The sign often says 'patika' (from Latin 'apotheca') instead; both are understood.
Adjective 'sick' and noun 'patient'. 'Beteg vagyok' = I'm ill; 'betegség' = illness; 'beteget jelent' = calls in sick.
'Egész' (whole) + -ség (-ness) + -es: health is 'wholeness'. 'Egészség' = health, 'Egészségedre' = cheers / bless you.
The thing that hurts is the subject: 'fáj a fejem' = my head hurts (literally 'hurts the head-my'). 'Fájdalom' = pain; 'fájdalomcsillapító' = painkiller.
'Lázas vagyok' = I have a fever. 'Lázmérő' (fever-measurer) = thermometer. Also 'fever' in the figurative sense: 'aranyláz' = gold rush.
The possessed noun carries the possessive ending ('fejem' = my head), with the article 'a' in front, and no verb 'have'. Swap in any body part: 'fáj a hátam', 'fáj a lábam'.
Cognate with Finnish 'veri'. Appears in 'testvér' (sibling), 'vérnyomás' (blood pressure) and 'vörös' (deep red).
A Finno-Ugric word related to Finnish 'kota' (hut). The á shortens before some suffixes: 'házak', 'házam'. 'Otthon' is home as a feeling; 'ház' is the building.
From 'lakik' (to dwell) + -ás. 'Lakásban lakom' = I live in a flat. 'Kiadó lakás' = flat to rent.

example.en: We live in a two-room flat.

note: A Slavic loan (compare Croatian 'soba'), ultimately related to German 'Stube'. Flats are counted by rooms: 'háromszobás' = three-room. 'Hálószoba' = bedroom.
A Slavic loan (compare Slovak 'kuchyňa'), ultimately from Latin 'coquina'. 'A konyhában' = in the kitchen; 'magyar konyha' = Hungarian cuisine.
'Fürdő' (bath, bathing, from 'fürdik' to bathe) + 'szoba'. The toilet is usually separate: 'WC' (pronounced 'vé-cé') or 'mosdó'.
The ó shortens before suffixes: 'ajtót', 'ajtók'. 'Az ajtóban' = in the doorway; 'bejárati ajtó' = front door.
A Slavic loan (compare Slovak 'oblok', from a root meaning 'round'). 'Az ablakban' = at the window; 'ablakot nyit' = opens a window.
'Ágyban' = in bed; 'lefekszik' = goes to bed (lies down). The 'gy' is one soft sound. 'Ágynemű' = bedding.
Also 'seat' in the sense of headquarters: 'székhely', and in the county name 'Székesfehérvár' (seat-white-castle). 'Széken ül' = sits on a chair.
A Slavic loan (compare Slovak 'kľúč'). The 'cs' is 'ch'. 'Kulcsot' (acc.); 'kulcsszó' = keyword.
From German 'Lampe'. Also a traffic light: 'piros a lámpa' = the light is red. 'Zseblámpa' (pocket-lamp) = torch.
Short for 'hűtőszekrény' (cooling-cupboard); 'hűt' = to cool, from 'hűs' (cool). 'A hűtőben' = in the fridge.
The letters T-V spelled out as Hungarian pronounces them; the full word is 'televízió'. 'Tévét néz' = watches TV.
From the same root as 'kerít' (to fence in) and 'kerek' (round): an enclosed plot. 'A kertben' = in the garden; 'kertész' = gardener.
From 'emel' (to lift) + -et. The ground floor is 'földszint' (ground-level), so 'első emelet' is one floor up, like British usage.

example.en: I live on the third floor.

note: 'Hol laksz?' = where do you live? Most Hungarian towns take -n/-on/-en ('Budapesten lakom'), foreign ones -ban/-ben ('Bécsben', in Vienna). 'Él' is 'to live' in the sense of being alive.
'Főzelék' is the thick vegetable stew that Hungarians eat as a main course. Definite: 'főzöm a levest'. 'Szakács' = cook (person).
'Mos' is for clothes and things; 'mosakszik' is to wash oneself and 'mosogat' is to wash dishes. 'Mosógép' = washing machine. 2nd person 'mosol' because the stem ends in -s.
Verbs in -ít take linking vowels: 'takarítasz', 'takarítanak'. 'Takarítónő' = cleaning lady; 'kitakarít' = to clean up completely.
Irregular -ik verb: infinitive 'aludni', past 'aludtam', so the stem swaps between 'alsz-' and 'alud-'. 'Jól aludtál?' = did you sleep well?
'Ott' (there) + 'hon' (homeland). When the speaker is actually at home it becomes 'itthon' (here-home). 'Otthonos' = cosy, homely.
'A falon' = on the wall. Also the verb 'to devour' ('fal'). Do not confuse with 'falu' (village).
The second ö drops before suffixes: 'tükröt', 'tükrök'. 'Tükörtojás' (mirror-egg) = fried egg sunny side up.
From Latin 'scrinium' (chest) via German. Any cupboard: 'hűtőszekrény' = fridge, 'ruhásszekrény' = wardrobe, 'könyvszekrény' = bookcase.
'A polcon' = on the shelf; 'könyvespolc' = bookshelf. Final 'c' = 'ts'.
A Slavic loan. Means both a woman's dress and clothing in general ('ruhák' = clothes). 'Ruhabolt' = clothes shop; 'fürdőruha' = swimsuit.
'Inget' (acc.), 'ingem' = my shirt. 'Rövid ujjú ing' = short-sleeved shirt ('ujj' = sleeve and also finger).
A Slavic loan. Singular in Hungarian: 'egy nadrág' = a pair of trousers. 'Rövidnadrág' = shorts, 'farmernadrág' = jeans.
A Slavic loan (compare Croatian 'suknja'). 'Miniszoknya' = miniskirt. The 'ny' is one palatal sound.
Singular for the pair: 'egy pár cipő'. 'Cipőbolt' = shoe shop, 'cipőfűző' = shoelace. Shoes come off at the door in most Hungarian homes.
From German 'Socken' with the Hungarian -i ending common in borrowed everyday words ('bicikli', 'krumpli').
A Slavic loan. 'Télikabát' = winter coat, 'esőkabát' = raincoat. Hungarian cloakrooms ('ruhatár') are often compulsory in theatres.
From English 'pullover', spelled the Hungarian way with a long ó. 'Kötött pulóver' = knitted sweater.
From 'polo shirt', but in Hungarian it means any T-shirt. 'Pólót' (acc.).
A Slavic loan (compare Russian 'shapka'). Any soft or knitted hat; a hat with a brim is 'kalap'. 'Baseballsapka' = baseball cap.
From German 'Schal', pronounced 'shaal'. 'Sálat' (acc.). A thin headscarf is 'kendő'.
Built on 'kéz' (hand), which appears as 'kesz-'. Usually singular for the pair: 'egy pár kesztyű'.
'Övet' (acc.), 'biztonsági öv' = seatbelt. Unrelated to 'övé' (his / hers) despite the look.
A false friend: 'farmer' means jeans (short for 'farmernadrág', 'farmer trousers', after the American farmers who wore them). A farmer is 'gazda' or 'farmer' with context.
From German 'Tasche'. Any bag from handbag to schoolbag; 'hátizsák' (back-sack) = backpack, 'pénztárca' = wallet.
'Szem' (eye) + 'üveg' (glass, bottle). Singular: 'egy szemüveg'. 'Napszemüveg' (sun-eye-glass) = sunglasses.
From 'mér' (to measure) + -et. 'Milyen méret?' = what size? 'Van nagyobb méretben?' = do you have it in a bigger size?

example.en: Do you have this in a bigger size?

note: 'Fel' (up) + 'vesz' (take). Also 'to record' and 'to answer the phone' ('felveszi a telefont'). Prefix detaches under focus: 'Mit veszel fel?' = What are you putting on?
'To carry' in general and, by extension, to wear habitually: 'szemüveget hord' = wears glasses. 'Visel' is the more formal 'to wear'.
'Le' (down) + 'vesz' (take), the opposite of 'felvesz'. Imperative: 'vedd le' (take it off), with the irregular stem 'ved-'.
'Divatos' = fashionable; 'divatban van' = is in fashion; 'kiment a divatból' = went out of fashion.
From Ottoman Turkish 'cep', one of the Turkish-era loans. 'Zsebpénz' = pocket money, 'zsebtolvaj' = pickpocket, 'zsebkendő' = handkerchief.
Also a knob or a push-button ('nyomd meg a gombot' = press the button). Not to be confused with 'gomba' (mushroom).
From Ottoman Turkish 'çizme'. The traditional high leather boot of hussars and folk dancers; 'bakancs' is a hiking or work boot.
'Fürdő' (bathing) + 'ruha'. Needed for Budapest's thermal baths ('gyógyfürdő'); 'fürdőnadrág' = swimming trunks.
A Slavic loan from a word meaning 'torment, toil' (compare Russian 'muka'). 'Munkahely' = workplace, 'munkanélküli' = unemployed. 'Munkát keres' = looks for a job.

example.en: I have a lot of work.

note: A reform-era coinage from 'ír' (to write) + -oda, like 'szálloda'. 'Az irodában' = at the office; 'utazási iroda' = travel agency.
'Fő' (head, chief) + the reform suffix -nök, also seen in 'elnök' (president) and 'mérnök' (engineer). 'Főnöknő' = female boss.
From Latin 'collega'. 'Kolléganő' = female colleague. 'Munkatárs' (work-companion) is the native synonym.
From 'tan' (doctrine, learning), the root of 'tanul' and 'tanít'. Female teachers are 'tanárnő', and pupils address them as 'Tanárnő!' or 'Tanár úr!'.
From Latin 'diaconus' via Slavic, where it meant 'clerk, scholar'. Covers pupils and university students; 'hallgató' (listener) is the formal word for the latter.
From Latin 'schola' via Slavic 'škola', with the i- added because Old Hungarian avoided initial sk-. 'Iskolába jár' = goes to school; 'suli' is the slang form.
A reform coinage from 'egy' (one) + -etem, a calque of Latin 'universitas'. 'Egyetemre jár' = attends university; 'egyetemista' = university student.
From 'tan'. 'Magyarul tanulok' = I'm learning Hungarian (the -ul suffix makes 'in Hungarian'). Definite: 'tanulom a szavakat'.
Same root as 'tanul'; the -ít ending makes a causative ('cause to learn'). Takes linking vowels: 'tanítasz', 'tanítanak'. 'Tanító' = primary school teacher.
From 'dolog' (thing, matter, work; a Slavic loan) + -oz + -ik. 'Hol dolgozol?' = where do you work? 'Dolgozó' = worker.
Also the adjective 'Irish' ('ír sör' = Irish beer). Definite: 'írom a levelet'. 'Író' = writer, 'írás' = writing.
Stem ends in -s, so 2nd person is 'olvasol'. Definite: 'olvasom a könyvet'. 'Olvasó' = reader; 'elolvas' = to read through (completed).
'Könyvtár' (book-store) = library, 'könyvesbolt' = bookshop. The final -nyv cluster takes a linking vowel: 'könyvet', 'könyvek'.
One word for 'feather' and 'pen', from the days of quills. 'Golyóstoll' (ball-pen) = ballpoint. 'Tollat' (acc.).
From German 'Papier'. Also 'document' in the plural: 'papírok' = papers, ID. 'Papírzsebkendő' = tissue.
From Latin 'lectio' (reading). A chapter in a textbook or the homework set from it: 'megcsinálom a leckét' = I'll do my homework. 'Házi feladat' is the formal 'homework'.
Back-formed from 'vizsgál' (to examine). 'Vizsgázik' = to sit an exam; 'nyelvvizsga' = language exam, which Hungarian degrees usually require.
Like French 'langue', one word for the tongue and a language. 'Magyar nyelv' = the Hungarian language, 'nyelvtan' = grammar, 'anyanyelv' = mother tongue.
The ó turns into 'av' before many suffixes: 'szavak' (words), 'szavam' (my word). 'Szótár' (word-store) = dictionary; 'szóval' = so, in a word.
From 'mond' (to say) + -at. A court sentence is 'ítélet', not 'mondat'.
'Számító' (computing, from 'szám' number) + 'gép' (machine). Often shortened to just 'gép'; 'laptop' is used as is.
'Szín' (stage, as in 'színház' theatre) + the profession suffix -ész. Female: 'színésznő'.
From 'fizet' (to pay) + -és. Means both the act of paying and one's salary. 'Fizetésemelés' = pay rise.
From 'megbeszél' (to discuss, 'meg-' + 'beszél' speak) + -és. 'Értekezlet' is a more formal staff meeting; 'meeting' is also borrowed in offices.
From 'esik' (to fall) + -ő: 'esik az eső' is literally 'the falling thing falls'. 'Esős' = rainy; 'esernyő' = umbrella (rain-shade).
The ó becomes 'av' before suffixes: 'havas' (snowy), 'havazik' (it's snowing). The same 'hó' means 'month' in dates ('hónap').
Also 'edge, side' ('az asztal szélén' = on the edge of the table). The é shortens: 'szelek', 'szeles' (windy). 'Fúj a szél' = the wind is blowing.
'Felhős' = cloudy; 'felhőszakadás' (cloud-tearing) = cloudburst. The final ő shortens: 'felhők'.
A Slavic loan (compare Croatian 'vihor', whirlwind). 'Viharos' = stormy; 'zivatar' is a thunderstorm.
'Meleg van' = it's warm / hot (no 'it'). 'Melegem van' = I'm hot. Also the everyday word for 'gay'. 'Forró' is 'scalding hot' for liquids.
'Hideg van' = it's cold; 'fázom' = I'm cold (a separate verb, 'fázik'). 'Hidegfront' = cold front.
'Esik' alone means 'it's raining' ('esik az eső'). Also 'to fall': 'elesik' = falls over, 'eső' = rain. -ik verb: 'esem' = I fall.
'Fúj a szél' = the wind is blowing; also 'to blow one's nose' ('orrot fúj') and the interjection 'fúj!' = yuck!
'Süt a nap' = the sun is shining, but 'kenyeret süt' = bakes bread and 'húst süt' = fries meat: one verb for heat from sun, oven or pan. 'Sütemény' = pastry.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'puu'. Means both the tree and the material: 'fából' = made of wood. 'Fák' = trees; 'almafa' = apple tree.
'Virágzik' = to bloom; 'virágbolt' = florist. A common girl's name is 'Virág'. 'Virágot' (acc.).
'Az erdőben' = in the forest; 'erdész' = forester. Transylvania is 'Erdély', from 'erdő elve' (beyond the forest), the same idea as Latin 'Transsilvania'.
Any hill or mountain; Budapest's 'Gellért-hegy' is a hill. Also the 'tip' of a pen or knife ('hegyes' = pointed). 'A hegyen' = on the mountain.
The participle of 'folyik' (to flow). The Danube is 'a Duna', the Tisza 'a Tisza'; river names take the article.
The ó becomes 'av' before suffixes: 'tavak' (lakes), 'a tavon' (on the lake). Lake Balaton is 'a Balaton', the 'Hungarian sea'.
An Old Turkic loan (compare Turkish 'deniz'). Hungary is landlocked, so 'a magyar tenger' (the Hungarian sea) is a fond name for Lake Balaton. 'Tengerpart' = seaside.
Also the verb 'to burn' ('ég a tűz' = the fire is burning). 'Az égen' = in the sky; 'égbolt' = the vault of the sky.
'Kutyaidő' (dog-weather) = foul weather; 'kutyául' = terribly ('kutyául érzem magam' = I feel awful). 'Eb' is the old literary word, as in 'ebadó' (dog tax).
A Slavic loan (compare Slovak 'mačka'). 'Cica' is the affectionate 'kitty'. 'Macskát' (acc.).
The á shortens before suffixes: 'madarak', 'madaram'. 'Madárlátta kenyér' (bread seen by birds) is food brought back home from a trip.
'Nyáron' = in summer; 'nyaral' = to holiday, 'nyári' = summer (adj.). The á shortens: 'nyarak'.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'talvi'. 'Télen' = in winter; the é shortens: 'telek', 'telet'. 'Téli' = winter (adj.).
'Tavasszal' = in spring (with -val/-vel, unlike the other seasons). 'Tavaszi' = spring (adj.).
Cognate with Finnish 'syksy'. Also the adjective 'grey-haired' ('ősz haj'). 'Ősszel' = in autumn; 'őszi' = autumn (adj.).
From Italian 'volta' (vault): medieval shops were vaulted ground-floor rooms. 'Boltban' = in the shop; 'üzlet' is the slightly more formal 'shop, business'.
From Italian 'piazza'. Budapest's Great Market Hall is 'a Nagy Vásárcsarnok'. 'A piacon' = at the market.

example.en: I buy vegetables at the market.

note: A Slavic loan ('penez', coin), itself from Germanic 'pfennig / penny'. 'Nincs pénzem' = I have no money; 'pénztárca' = wallet.
From Italian 'fiorino', the Florentine gold florin; Hungary's currency since 1946. Abbreviated 'Ft'; the slang 'ezres' = a thousand-forint note.
Also 'flood' and 'awl'; context decides. 'Árak' = prices, 'féláron' = at half price, 'árcédula' = price tag.
A Slavic loan (compare Croatian 'drag'). Like English 'dear', it is also a term of endearment: 'drágám' = my darling.
'Olcsóbb' = cheaper; 'olcsón' = cheaply. The 'cs' is 'ch'.
Means 'take' and, from that, 'buy'. Irregular: infinitive 'venni', past 'vettem'. Definite: 'megveszem' = I'll buy it. 'Kenyeret veszek' = I'm buying bread.
From 'vásár' (market), so literally 'to market'. 'Bevásárol' = to do the shopping; 'vásárló' = customer. More formal than 'vesz'.
Basic meaning 'to get somewhere, to end up'; a price is where the thing 'comes to'. Takes -ba/-be: 'ezer forintba kerül' = it costs 1000 Ft. Also 'to avoid' with an object.
'El' (away) + 'ad' (give). The prefix separates: 'nem adom el' = I'm not selling it. 'Eladó' = for sale, and also the shop assistant.
'Mennyi' (how much) + -be (into) + 'kerül'. The casual alternative is 'Mennyi?' or 'Mennyibe van?'. Answers come with -ba/-be: 'kétezerbe' (2000).
'Bankban dolgozik' = works in a bank; 'bankautomata' or 'ATM' (pronounced 'á-té-em') = cash machine.
'Bank' + 'kártya' (card, from Latin 'charta'). 'Kártyával fizetek' = I'll pay by card; 'érintéses' = contactless.
'Kész' (ready) + 'pénz' (money), exactly the old English 'ready money'. 'Készpénzzel' = in cash.
'Pénz' + 'tár' (store), as in 'könyvtár' (library). 'A pénztárnál' = at the checkout; 'pénztáros' = cashier; 'jegypénztár' = ticket office.
A false friend: in shops 'akció' means a discount or promotion, not 'action'. 'Akciós' = on offer; 'Akció!' is the sign to look for.
From 'nyit' (to open) + -va, a form that describes a resulting state. 'Nyitva tartás' = opening hours. The adjective 'nyitott' is 'open-minded' or 'open' as a quality.

example.en: Is it open on Sunday too?

note: From 'zár' (to close, to lock; also the noun 'lock') + -va. 'Zárva van' = it's closed. 'Zárás' = closing time.
'Ajándékba' = as a present; 'ajándékoz' = to give as a gift; 'ajándékbolt' = gift shop.
A Slavic loan. The á shortens: 'kosarat', 'kosarak'. 'Kosárlabda' (basket-ball) = basketball; 'kosarat ad' (gives a basket) = turns down a suitor.
The soft bag you carry shopping in; the o drops before suffixes: 'szatyrot', 'szatyrok'. 'Zacskó' is a small plastic or paper bag.
The participle of 'elad'. As a noun, the person who sells; on a sign, 'Eladó' = for sale. 'Eladónő' = saleswoman.
'Áru' (goods, merchandise) + 'ház' (house). 'Bevásárlóközpont' (shopping-centre) = mall, 'pláza' colloquially.
'Kérek egy nyugtát' = may I have a receipt. Shops are legally required to give one; 'blokk' is the colloquial till slip, 'számla' a formal invoice.
'Boldog születésnapot!' = Happy birthday! 'Boldog új évet!' = Happy New Year! 'Boldogság' = happiness.
'Szomorúság' = sadness; 'szomorúan' = sadly; 'szomorúfűz' (sad willow) = weeping willow. 'Ne légy szomorú!' = don't be sad.
The past participle of 'fárad' (to tire). 'Fáradt vagyok' = I'm tired; 'elfáradtam' = I've got tired. 'Fáradjon be!' = please come in (formal), literally 'tire yourself in'.

example.en: I'm tired, I'm going to bed.

note: From 'éh' (hunger, as in 'éhség') + -es. 'Éhes vagyok' = I'm hungry; 'éhen hal' = starves to death.
From 'szomj' (thirst) + -as. 'Szomjas vagyok' = I'm thirsty; 'szomjúság' = thirst.
From 'méreg' (poison) + -es: anger as poison in the blood. 'Mérges vagyok rád' = I'm angry with you (-ra/-re). 'Dühös' is the stronger 'furious'.
From 'ideg' (nerve) + -es. Covers both 'anxious' and 'irritated': 'ne légy ideges' = don't be nervous / don't get worked up.
The past participle of 'nyugszik' (to rest). 'Nyugodtan' = calmly, and as a reply 'go ahead, feel free'. 'Nyugalom!' = calm down!
From 'szerelem' (romantic love) + -es. Takes -ba/-be: 'szerelmes vagyok beléd' = I'm in love with you.
Covers both 'like' and 'love': 'szeretem a kávét' = I like coffee (definite). With an infinitive = 'like to': 'szeretek olvasni'. 'Szeretnék' = I would like.
An -ik verb: 'aggódom' = I'm worried. Takes -ért: 'aggódom érted' = I'm worried about you. 'Ne aggódj!' = don't worry.
Takes -nak/-nek: 'örülök neki' = I'm glad about it; 'Örülök, hogy...' = I'm glad that... 'Öröm' = joy, 'örömmel' = with pleasure.
The same word is the noun 'grave' ('sírkő' = gravestone). 'Ne sírj!' = don't cry. 'Sírás' = crying.
'Nevet valamin' = laughs at something (-n). 'Nevetés' = laughter; 'mosolyog' = to smile. 'Kinevet' = to laugh at someone (mock).
Definite with a specific object: 'utálom a hideget' = I hate the cold. 'Gyűlöl' is the stronger, more literary 'to loathe'.
The second e drops before vowel endings: 'érzek', 'érzel', but 'érez', 'éreznek'. 'Hogy érzed magad?' = How do you feel? (reflexive 'magad' = yourself). 'Érzés' = feeling.
'Remélem, hogy...' (definite) = I hope that... 'Remény' = hope (noun); 'reménytelen' = hopeless.
Same root as 'örül' (to be glad). The second ö drops: 'örömöt' or 'örömet', 'örömmel' (gladly). 'Örömhír' = good news.
Romantic love only; love for family, food or country is 'szeretet'. The e drops: 'szerelmet', 'szerelmes'. 'Első szerelem' = first love.
From 'un' (to be tired of) with the reflexive -kozik: 'unatkozom' = I'm bored. 'Unalmas' = boring; 'unom' = I'm fed up with it.
One word: the ending -lak/-lek is a special form meaning 'I ... you', used only when 'I' acts on 'you'. 'Látlak' = I see you, 'hívlak' = I'll call you.
Hungarian turns it round: 'you are lacking (to me)', from 'hiányzik' (to be missing) in the 2nd person. 'Hiányzol nekem' adds the 'to me'. 'Hiány' = lack.
'Jó' (good) + 'kedv' (mood, liking) + -ű (having). 'Rosszkedvű' = in a bad mood; 'jó kedvem van' = I'm in a good mood.
'Boldog' + the abstract suffix -ság/-ség, which follows vowel harmony (boldogság, but egészség). 'Sok boldogságot!' = congratulations (to a couple).
The past participle of 'meglep' (to surprise), from 'lep' (to cover) with the prefix 'meg-'. 'Meglepetés' = a surprise.
A Slavic loan (compare Slovak 'činiť'). 'Mit csinálsz?' = What are you doing? Definite: 'csinálom' = I'm doing it. 'Megcsinál' = to get it done.

en: to know / to be able to
note: Both 'know' (a fact or skill) and 'can': 'tudok úszni' = I can swim. 'Nem tudom' = I don't know (definite). Finno-Ugric, related to Finnish 'tuntea'.
Blunt in requests; prefer 'szeretnék' (I would like). 'Mit akarsz?' can sound like 'what do you want from me?'. Definite: 'akarom'.
'Látom' (definite) = I see it / I see. 'Viszontlátásra' contains it: 'until seeing again'. 'Látogat' = to visit.
Stem ends in -z, so 2nd person is 'nézel'. 'Tévét néz' = watches TV; 'nézz ide' = look here. 'Megnéz' = to take a look at, to check.
The double -ll needs linking vowels: 'hallasz', 'hallanak'. 'Hallgat' = to listen (and 'to keep silent'!). 'Halló?' on the phone is from this verb.
From the Slavic loan 'beszéd' (speech). Languages take -ul/-ül: 'beszélek magyarul' = I speak Hungarian. 'Beszélget' = to chat.
The -nd cluster needs linking vowels: 'mondasz', 'mondanak'. Definite 'mondom' = I say (it); 'Mondd!' = tell me! 'Mondat' = sentence.

example.en: How do you say it in Hungarian?

note: Recipient takes -nak/-nek: 'adok neked' = I give you. Definite: 'adom'. 'Elad' = sell, 'felad' = post / give up, 'kiad' = rent out.
'Kapok egy levelet' = I get a letter. 'Kapható' = available (can be got). 'Elkap' = to catch; 'megkap' = to receive (completed).

example.en: What did you get for your birthday?

note: Movement toward the speaker; 'visz' is away. Stem ends in -z: 'hozol'. Also the suffix -hoz/-hez/-höz ('to'), which is a different word.

example.en: Will you bring me a coffee?

note: Irregular like 'vesz' and 'eszik': infinitive 'vinni', past 'vittem'. 'Elvisz' = to take away; 'elvitelre' = takeaway.
Also the noun 'chin'. 'Megáll' = to stop, 'megálló' = bus stop. 'Jól áll neked' = it suits you (it stands well on you).
'Leül' = to sit down; 'Ülj le!' = sit down! 'Ülés' = seat (and a session). 'Üljön le, kérem' is the formal invitation.
'Futok' = I run / I go running; 'futás' = running. 'Elfut' = runs away. Also of trains and time: 'fut az idő' = time flies.
From 'játék' (game, toy). An -ik verb: 'játszom'. Takes -val/-vel for a game or partner: 'focival játszik', 'a gyerekekkel játszik'.

example.en: The children are playing in the park.

note: The person helped takes -nak/-nek: 'segítek neked' = I help you. 'Segítség!' = Help! 'Tudok segíteni?' = Can I help?
'Kinyit' = to open (fully); 'nyitva' = open (sign). Definite: 'kinyitom az ablakot'. 'Zár' is the opposite, 'to close'.
Both 'to call' by phone and 'to name': 'Hogy hívnak?' = what's your name? 'Felhív' = to phone; 'meghív' = to invite.
'Gondolom' (definite) = I think so / I suppose. 'Gondol valamire' = thinks of something (-ra/-re). 'Gondolat' = a thought; 'gondolkodik' = to ponder.
The -rt cluster needs linking vowels: 'értesz', 'értenek'. 'Értem' (definite) = I understand; 'Nem értem' = I don't understand. Also 'to reach, arrive' ('ér').
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'elää'. 'Élet' = life, 'élő' = living. 'Hol élsz?' asks where you have your life; 'lakik' is just where you reside.
The -zd cluster needs linking vowels: 'kezdesz', 'kezdenek'. 'Elkezd' = to start (something); 'kezdődik' = to begin (of an event). 'Kezdet' = beginning.
'Ismer' is to be acquainted with; 'tud' is to know a fact. 'Ismerem őt' = I know him/her. 'Megismer' = to get to know; 'ismerős' = acquaintance / familiar.
'Itt maradok' = I'm staying here. 'Maradék' = leftovers; 'Maradj!' = stay! 'Otthon marad' = stays at home.
'Mi' is also the pronoun 'we' ('mi vagyunk' = we are). Accusative 'mit': 'Mit kérsz?' = What would you like? 'Mi ez?' = What is this?
Also the verb prefix 'out' ('kimegy' = goes out). Accusative 'kit', dative 'kinek' (to whom). 'Ki az?' = Who is it?
Hungarian separates 'where' (hol), 'where to' (hova / hová) and 'where from' (honnan). 'Hova mész?' = Where are you going?
The 'from' member of the hol / hova / honnan trio. 'Honnan jössz?' = Where are you coming from? 'Honnan tudod?' = How do you know?
'Mikor indul?' = When does it leave? The relative 'when' adds a-: 'amikor' (at the time when). 'Mióta?' = since when?
'Mi' (what) + -ért (for the sake of). The answer starts with 'mert' (because) or 'azért, mert'. Colloquially shortened to 'mér'.
'Hogy' is the short form ('Hogy vagy?') and also the conjunction 'that'. 'Hogyan mondják?' = How do you say it?
'Mi' + -lyen. 'Milyen az idő?' = What's the weather like? 'Milyen színű?' = What colour? Also an exclamation: 'Milyen szép!' = How beautiful!
'Melyik busz megy a központba?' = Which bus goes to the centre? Accusative 'melyiket'. The relative form is 'amelyik'.
'Mennyi' = how much (uncountable or a price); 'hány' = how many. 'Mennyi az idő?' = What's the time? 'Mennyibe kerül?' = How much is it?
Often shortened to 's' in speech and writing ('te s én'). No comma before 'és' in a plain list; 'meg' is a colloquial 'and' for two items ('kenyér meg vaj').
Identical to 'vagy' = 'you are' ('Hol vagy?' = Where are you?). 'Vagy... vagy...' = either... or... 'Kávé vagy tea?'

example.en: Would you like coffee or tea?

note: Also an intensifier at the start of exclamations: 'De szép!' = How beautiful! 'De jó!' = Great! 'Hanem' is 'but' after a negative ('nem én, hanem ő').
Comes after a comma: 'Nem megyek, mert fáradt vagyok.' 'Miért? – Mert.' ('Why? – Because.') works in Hungarian as in English.

example.en: I'm not going because I'm ill.

note: Always placed right after the word it belongs to: 'én is' = me too, 'ma is' = today as well. Not the English 'is'; 'Én is kérek' = I'd like some too.
'Csak egy' = just one; 'csak most' = only now. Also a softener: 'Csak kérdezem' = I'm just asking. Pronounced 'chok'.
'Nagy' (big) + the adverb ending -on. 'Nagyon jó' = very good; 'nagyon köszönöm' = thanks a lot. 'Nem nagyon' = not really.
'Már nem' = no longer; 'már megint' = yet again. Softens requests: 'Gyere már!' = Come on, then!
'Még nem' = not yet; 'még egy' = one more; 'még mindig' = still. Pairs with 'már' (already): 'még' looks forward, 'már' back.
'Mind' (all) + -ig (until): 'all the way through'. 'Mindig is' = always has been. 'Minden' = every / everything shares the root.
Needs the double negative: 'soha nem' or 'sohasem'. 'Soha nem késik' = he is never late. 'Soha többé' = never again.
With a noun the article is repeated: 'ez a ház' = this house. Accusative 'ezt'; the z assimilates before suffixes: 'ebben' (in this), 'erre' (onto this). 'Az' = that.
Impersonal: 'kell egy jegy' = a ticket is needed; 'mennem kell' = I must go (infinitive with personal ending). 'Nem kell' = no need / I don't want it.
The negative of 'van' (there is); 'nem van' is never said. 'Nincs pénzem' = I have no money (literally 'is-not money-my'). Plural 'nincsenek'.
'Talán holnap' = maybe tomorrow. 'Lehet' (it is possible) is the other common 'maybe' in replies.
Comparative 'nagyobb', superlative 'legnagyobb'. 'Nagyon' (very) is its adverb; 'nagymama', 'nagybácsi' use it for 'grand-'.
'Kicsi' stands alone or after the noun; before a noun the short form 'kis' is usual: 'kis ház'. Comparative 'kisebb'. 'Kicsit' = a little (adverb).
Irregular comparative 'jobb' (also 'right-hand'), superlative 'legjobb'. 'Jól' = well. Appears in every greeting: 'jó napot', 'jó éjszakát'.
Comparative 'rosszabb'. 'Rosszul' = badly, 'rosszul vagyok' = I feel unwell. The double 'ssz' is a long 's' sound.
Comparative 'szebb' (the é shortens and -bb attaches directly). 'Szépen' = nicely, as in 'köszönöm szépen'. 'Szépség' = beauty.
Also 'nasty' of weather or words: 'csúnya idő' = foul weather, 'csúnyán beszél' = uses bad language.
Finno-Ugric cognate of Finnish 'uusi'. 'Boldog új évet!' = Happy New Year. 'Újra' = again, 'újság' (new-ness) = newspaper.
From 'rég' (long ago) + -i. For things and times only; an old person is 'öreg' or 'idős'. 'Régen' = long ago, 'régóta' = for a long time.
Comparative 'fiatalabb'. 'Fiatalok' = young people. Related to 'fiú' (boy, son) in its first syllable.
For people and animals; 'idős' is the polite 'elderly'. 'Öregem!' = old chap! 'Régi' is 'old' for objects.
Comparative 'hosszabb' (the ú drops). 'Hosszú' is for length; 'hosszú ideig' = for a long time.
Both for length and time: 'rövid haj' = short hair, 'röviden' = briefly. A short person is 'alacsony', not 'rövid'.
One word for tall people and high things: 'magas ház', 'magas ár' (high price). Comparative 'magasabb'. 'Magasság' = height.
The opposite of 'magas': 'alacsony ember' = a short person, 'alacsony ár' = a low price. The 'cs' is 'ch' and 'ny' is palatal.
'Gyorsan' = quickly; 'gyorsvonat' = express train; 'gyorsétterem' = fast-food restaurant. Comparative 'gyorsabb'.
Comparative 'lassabb' (the ú drops). 'Lassan' = slowly: 'Lassabban, kérem' = slower, please. 'Lassan' also means 'gradually, soon'.
From 'erő' (strength) + -s. Also 'spicy' of food: 'erős paprika' = hot paprika, 'erős' on a menu means hot.
Of people, coffee, arguments or a wifi signal: 'gyenge a kávé' = the coffee is weak. 'Gyengébb' = weaker.
One word for 'light in weight' and 'easy', like French 'léger'. Comparative 'könnyebb'. 'Könnyen' = easily.
Both 'heavy' and 'difficult': 'nehéz nyelv' = a hard language. The é shortens in 'nehezebb' (harder) and 'nehezen' (with difficulty).
A Slavic loan (compare Croatian 'čist'). Also 'pure, clear': 'tiszta víz', 'tiszta sor' (clear case). Colloquially an intensifier: 'tiszta hülye' = totally stupid.
From 'piszok' (dirt) + -os; the o drops. 'Koszos' is the everyday synonym. 'Piszkos munka' = dirty work.
From 'érdek' (interest, concern) + -es. 'Érdekel' = it interests me (the thing is the subject). 'Érdekes!' on its own means 'How odd!'.
From 'font' (pound, the unit of weight) + -os: something that has weight. 'Fontosabb' = more important; 'nem fontos' = never mind.
From 'ok' (reason, cause) + -os. 'Okostelefon' = smartphone. 'Buta' = stupid; 'bölcs' = wise.
From 'vár' (castle) + -os: a town grew up beneath a castle. 'Városban' = in town; 'városháza' = town hall. Buda and Pest were united as one város in 1873.
'Falun' = in the village (with -n, like most Hungarian place names); 'falusi' = rural. The plural is irregular: 'falvak'.
'Fő' (head, main) + 'város'. 'A főváros' usually just means Budapest, home to about a fifth of Hungary's population.
'Bel' (inner) + 'város'. In Budapest 'Belváros' is also the name of district V on the Pest side. 'A belvárosban' = downtown.

example.en: I live in the city centre.

note: The í shortens before suffixes: 'hidak', 'hidat'. Budapest's bridges have names: 'Lánchíd' (Chain Bridge), 'Erzsébet híd', 'Szabadság híd' (Liberty Bridge).
From Latin 'templum'; used for any Christian church. 'Mátyás-templom' is the one on Castle Hill. 'Egyház' (one-house) is the Church as an institution.
Pronounced 'MOO-ze-um' with first-syllable stress. 'A Nemzeti Múzeum' = the National Museum; 'múzeumba megy' = goes to a museum.
'Szín' (stage; also 'colour') + 'ház'. 'Színházba megy' = goes to the theatre; 'színész' = actor.
Clipped from 'mozgókép' (moving picture) and popularised by the writer Heltai Jenő in 1907. 'Moziba megy' = goes to the cinema.

example.en: Shall we go to the cinema?

note: 'A parkban' = in the park. Budapest's 'Városliget' (city-grove) is the big park behind Heroes' Square.
'Könyv' (book) + 'tár' (repository), the same -tár as in 'szótár' (dictionary) and 'pénztár' (cash desk). 'Könyvtáros' = librarian.
From Italian 'posta'. 'A postán' = at the post office; 'postás' = postman. 'Feladni egy levelet' = to post a letter.
'Rend' (order) + 'őr' (guard) + -ség. 'Rendőr' = police officer. The emergency number is 112.
From 'fürdik' (to bathe) + -ő. Budapest's thermal baths (Széchenyi, Gellért, Rudas) are 'gyógyfürdő', healing baths; 'fürdőszoba' = bathroom.
'Margit-sziget' is the park island in the Danube; the 'Sziget' festival is held on 'Óbudai-sziget'. 'A szigeten' = on the island.
From 'épül' (to be built) + -et; 'épít' = to build, 'építész' = architect. 'Az épületben' = in the building.
From 'kerül' (to go round) + -et. Budapest has 23 districts, written in Roman numerals: 'a VII. kerület' (the seventh district). Addresses always give it.

example.en: Which district do you live in?

note: From Latin 'castellum' via German. A country house or palace (Gödöllő, Fertőd); a fortress is 'vár', as in 'Budai Vár' (Buda Castle).
'Benzin' + 'kút' (well). The ú shortens: 'benzinkutat', 'benzinkutak'. 'Tankol' = to fill up.
'Játszó' (playing, from 'játszik') + 'tér' (space, square). 'A játszótéren' = at the playground.
From 'temet' (to bury) + -ő. 'A temetőben' = in the cemetery. 'Temetés' = funeral.
The o drops before suffixes: 'tornyot', 'tornyok'. 'Templomtorony' = church tower; 'toronyház' = tower block.
An Old Turkic loanword (compare Turkish 'kapı', door). Budapest flats are reached through a street 'kapu' with a code ('kapukód'). Also 'goal' in football.
'Köz' (middle, common) + 'pont' (point). 'Városközpont' = town centre, 'bevásárlóközpont' = shopping centre, 'központi' = central.
From 'áll' (to stand) + -omás. Used for smaller railway stations and for 'metróállomás'; big terminals are 'pályaudvar'. 'Benzinkút' is a petrol station.
